name: Rapamycin

lead: Rapamycin (sirolimus) is a prescription immunosuppressant that some longevity enthusiasts use off-label to slow aging and keep a younger look, and it is explored topically for skin rejuvenation.

It inhibits mTORC1, a nutrient-sensing growth pathway, which promotes autophagy and reduces growth signaling. It is among the best-replicated lifespan-extending drugs in mice. A 2024 systematic review of 19 human studies found improvements in some physiological aging parameters in immune, cardiovascular and skin systems, with increased infections and raised cholesterol and triglycerides in people with age-related diseases. It is approved for transplant rejection, certain rare diseases and, topically, facial angiofibromas.

paras: Used only with a prescription, under physician supervision, off-label, and typically on an intermittent schedule in longevity communities, often with regular blood work. Topical forms are used in skin experiments.

Prescription-only. Known adverse effects include mouth ulcers, impaired wound healing, raised lipids, glucose intolerance and increased infection risk, particularly at transplant levels. Off-label use for longevity is not approved.

angle.text: Rapamycin inhibits mTOR, a growth pathway linked to aging, and users hope it keeps skin and body looking younger. Lifespan extension is shown in animals; it is an immunosuppressant with known side effects.

lead: Rapamycin, also called sirolimus and sold under the brand name Rapamune among others, is a macrolide compound produced by the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It was first isolated in the early 1970s from a soil sample taken on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), which gave the compound its name.[1] It was first studied as an antifungal, but its potent immunosuppressive and antiproliferative properties, which arise from inhibiting the kinase mTOR, redirected its development.[1][2]

It is a prescription drug used to prevent organ transplant rejection (particularly in kidney transplantation), to treat the rare lung disease lymphangioleiomyomatosis, to coat coronary stents, and, in a protein-bound form, to treat a rare tumour called PEComa. It is also used in vascular malformations and, topically, for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis complex.[1] Because inhibiting mTOR extends lifespan in several animal species, rapamycin has become the most discussed prescription drug in longevity communities, where some people use it off-label.[3][4]

Evidence for human anti-aging benefit remains preliminary. A 2024 Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review of 19 studies found improvements in some physiological parameters of ageing in immune, cardiovascular and skin systems, no significant effects on endocrine, muscular or neurological systems, and increased infections and raised cholesterol and triglycerides in people with age-related diseases.[3] A small exploratory trial of topical rapamycin reported reduced skin senescence markers,[5] but no trial has shown that rapamycin changes visible appearance or extends human lifespan.

Beyond ageing, rapamycin sits at the centre of two appearance-adjacent conversations: skin, because topical sirolimus treats disfiguring facial angiofibromas and a small trial examined skin senescence markers, and muscle, because the mTOR pathway it blocks is the same one that resistance training and amino acids switch on to build muscle.[1][5][6] Both topics are discussed in longevity and fitness communities, usually as questions rather than established results.

paras: In the United States sirolimus (Rapamune) is indicated to prevent rejection in renal transplant recipients aged 13 and older and to treat lymphangioleiomyomatosis, with the latter approval in May 2015 making it the first drug approved for that disease. A protein-bound formulation (Fyarro) is approved for advanced PEComa.[1][7] Its chief advantage over calcineurin inhibitors in transplantation is lower kidney toxicity.[1] In the EU, topical sirolimus (Hyftor) is approved for facial angiofibroma associated with tuberous sclerosis complex.[1]

Sirolimus-eluting coronary stents reduce restenosis compared with bare-metal stents, and sirolimus-coated balloons are being compared with paclitaxel-coated balloons.[1][8][9] Sirolimus is also used in vascular anomalies and has been studied in children with slow-flow vascular malformations in a randomised trial,[10] as well as in tuberous sclerosis complex[11] and epilepsy linked to focal cortical dysplasia.[12] Analogues such as temsirolimus are used in cancers such as renal cell carcinoma.[13]

The case for rapamycin in ageing rests on animal research showing lifespan extension and on the central role of mTOR in nutrient sensing, growth and autophagy.[14][15] Reviews describe mTOR as a regulator of ageing processes.[3][4] Some people take low-dose, intermittent off-label rapamycin under physician supervision. Some commentary in the community frames this as an attempt to slow ageing, including skin ageing, although no study has tested systemic rapamycin for appearance outcomes.

Topical use is a separate strand: a 2019 exploratory randomised trial in GeroScience tested topical rapamycin on human skin and examined markers of senescence and ageing.[5] A registered phase 2 trial is testing topical rapamycin for vitiligo.[16] Facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis are a disfiguring condition for which topical sirolimus has shown positive results in reviewed reports, with improvement in a large majority of the 84 patients described in one review cited by Wikipedia.[1]

Reduced TOR activity extends lifespan in yeast, nematodes and fruit flies, and evidence that TOR signalling regulates ageing in roundworms dates to around 2003.[6][17] Wikipedia's timeline records that in 2009 rapamycin was shown to extend lifespan in mice, and Wikipedia's mTOR article states that the National Institute on Aging's Interventions Testing Program and at least ten other groups had reported this effect by 2023, in both sexes and in inbred, outbred and genetically mixed mice.[6][17] The same article notes that, unlike caloric restriction, rapamycin still extended lifespan when started at 20 months of age, roughly 60 human years.[6] Wikipedia's sirolimus article adds that a 2020 study found late-life dosing extended lifespan in male but not female mice, and a 2022 timeline entry reports that limited-period dosing extended lifespan about as much as lifelong dosing, most effectively in early adulthood.[1][17]

In companion dogs, the Dog Aging Project, founded in 2014 at the University of Washington and directed by Daniel Promislow with Kate Creevy as chief veterinarian, runs the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled TRIAD trial of rapamycin in healthy middle-aged dogs, with lifespan and healthspan measures as endpoints; a separate 2017 ten-week trial in a small number of dogs reported better heart function than controls.[17][18] In humans, Wikipedia's sirolimus article says two human studies showed no statistically significant longevity benefit, with limitations noting that more research is needed, and describes topical use at concentrations far below those used for angiofibromas as reported to regenerate collagen and reverse clinical signs of skin ageing in elderly patients.[1] Wikipedia also records community self-experimentation with the related drug everolimus after a 2014 Novartis study.[1]

Sirolimus binds the cytosolic protein FKBP12, and that complex inhibits mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1), which is how it blocks T and B cell activation and signalling by interleukins such as IL-2.[1][19] This differs from tacrolimus, which forms a complex with the same binding protein but inhibits calcineurin.[1] The mTOR pathway integrates nutrient, growth-factor and energy signals to regulate growth, metabolism and autophagy, and has been implicated in cancer, diabetes and ageing.[20][14][15][21] Research has shown that AMPK and mTOR regulate autophagy through phosphorylation of Ulk1,[15] and that the rictor-containing mTOR complex phosphorylates Akt.[22] Longer exposure can also affect mTORC2, which Wikipedia links to diabetes-like effects such as reduced glucose tolerance; in mice such effects were avoided with alternative dosing regimens or analogues.[1]

Sirolimus is metabolised by CYP3A4 and is a substrate of the P-glycoprotein pump, so inhibitors of either may raise blood levels and inducers may lower them.[1] A registered study compared the bioavailability of compounded and generic rapamycin in people of normal ageing.[23]

The mTORC1 complex senses nutrients and energy and controls protein synthesis; Wikipedia states that its activation is required for myofibrillar protein synthesis and muscle hypertrophy in humans in response to exercise and to amino acids such as leucine, and that persistent mTORC1 inactivation contributes to muscle loss in ageing, cachexia and inactivity.[6] Resistance training stimulates muscle protein synthesis for up to 48 hours, and a protein-rich meal in that window augments the effect.[6] Bodybuilding forum threads refer to mTOR in this protein-synthesis sense, and because rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, some readers ask whether it would blunt training adaptations.[24][25][6] The 2024 systematic review of human rapamycin studies found no significant effect on the muscular system but did not examine training outcomes in detail, and no trial has tested rapamycin against hypertrophy in lifters.[3]

The US label carries a boxed warning for immunosuppression, with increased susceptibility to infection and possible development of lymphoma and other malignancies, and states that use is not recommended in liver or lung transplant patients.[26] Warnings and precautions in the label include hypersensitivity reactions, angioedema, fluid accumulation, impaired wound healing, hyperlipidaemia, decline in renal function, proteinuria, latent viral infections and interstitial lung disease or non-infectious pneumonitis.[26] The label also states that sirolimus can cause fetal harm based on animal studies and its mechanism.[26]

In transplant trials the most common adverse reactions include peripheral oedema, raised cholesterol and triglycerides, hypertension, raised creatinine, anaemia and infections; in lymphangioleiomyomatosis, mouth and lip ulcers, acne and diarrhoea were commonly reported.[1] Pulmonary toxicity is a recognised complication, particularly in lung transplant recipients, and the mechanism is unclear.[1] Sirolimus-induced lymphoedema has been described in case reports.[27] Wikipedia notes warnings that sirolimus may raise mortality in some transplant settings through infection risk, increased risk of skin cancer and lymphoma, and delayed wound healing, especially in people with BMI above 30.[1]

Longevity-related human studies. The 2024 Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review identified 19 studies from 18,400 articles and reported improvements in physiological parameters of ageing in the immune, cardiovascular and integumentary systems, but no significant effects on endocrine, muscular or neurological systems. It reported no serious adverse events attributed to rapamycin or rapalogs in healthy individuals but more infections and increases in total and LDL cholesterol and triglycerides in people with age-related diseases, and noted that long-term exposure has not been tested.[3] The PEARL randomised trial reported safety and healthspan metrics after one year of rapamycin dosing in healthy adults in Aging in 2025.[28] The 2019 topical study was exploratory and prospective, with senescence markers as the main outcome.[5]

Established indications. Randomised trials support use in transplantation, including a large trial of reduced calcineurin-inhibitor exposure in renal transplantation involving 1,645 recipients,[29] and in LAM, where a placebo-controlled trial in 89 patients for 12 months informed approval.[1] Registered trials cover topical rapamycin for angiofibromas in TSC (n=179),[30] Peutz-Jeghers syndrome,[31] venous malformations,[32] and uterine fibroids.[33] Glucocorticoid-free islet transplantation regimens using sirolimus were reported in seven patients in 2000.[34] A 2026 trial examined sirolimus-coated balloons in infrainguinal artery disease.[9]
No studies were found testing oral rapamycin for visible skin, hair or facial appearance in healthy people.

Rapamycin was isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus in soil collected on Easter Island; Wikipedia gives 1972 as the first isolation, while Grokipedia describes a 1964 expedition and a 1975 report from Ayerst Laboratories, now part of Pfizer.[1][7][2] It was developed first as an antifungal with strong activity against Candida, then abandoned for that use once its immunosuppressive and antiproliferative properties were recognised.[1][2][35] The FDA approved it on 15 September 1999 for kidney transplant rejection prophylaxis.[7] Research on its target, TOR, began with yeast mutants resistant to the drug, and the protein was later named mammalian target of rapamycin.[1] Landmark mTOR reviews now rank among the most-cited in the field.[14][21]

Surendra Nath Sehgal is credited in Wikipedia's mTOR article with isolating the compound in 1972, and the 1975 isolation paper lists him as co-author.[1][6] In 1991 Joseph Heitman, Rao Movva and Michael Hall identified the yeast genes TOR1 and TOR2, named for 'target of rapamycin'; in 1993 two groups cloned them, and in 1994 several groups showed that mTOR is the direct mammalian target. The mammalian protein was variously called FRAP and RAFT1 before the name mTOR became standard, and the gene symbol was officially changed to mTOR in 2009.[6]

Wikipedia dates the sirolimus approvals as Rapamune solution in 1999 and tablets in August 2000, Fyarro in November 2021, and topical Hyftor authorised in the EU in May 2023 after a positive EMA opinion in February 2023.[1]

Rapamycin is a prescription drug in the US, UK and EU, and use for ageing is off-label; community members describe obtaining it through physicians or compounding arrangements. On T Nation, forum members mention rapamycin alongside resveratrol and caloric restriction in discussions of life extension, with one 2010 post noting that direct TOR blocking is a heavy-handed approach because rapamycin strongly suppresses the immune system.[36][37] Many other T Nation threads mention mTOR only in the context of muscle protein synthesis and leucine, rather than the drug itself.[24][25]

Community use is discussed as intermittent off-label prescribing, obtained through physicians or compounding arrangements, as described above; the drug remains prescription-only. Public interest in rapamycin as a healthspan intervention follows the 2009 mouse results, the Dog Aging Project's trial and later human studies such as PEARL.[3][28][17][18]

lore.intro: In longevity circles rapamycin is treated as a leading candidate to slow ageing; community discussion on T Nation is sparse and often conflates the drug with the mTOR pathway.[36][37][24]
